extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, constitutional law, and comparative government; informed readers interested in judicial power and impeachment
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of the characteristics, rights, limits, and political effects of judicial power and political jurisdiction—especially the American practice of judicial review and impeachment—contrasted with French and English systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of arbitration (first characteristic of judicial power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first characteristic of judicial power is the duty of arbitration: rights must be contested and an action must be brought in order to warrant a tribunal's interference; as long as a law is uncontested the judicial authority is not called upon to discuss it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judge attacks a law in the context of a particular case he extends his customary duties but remains within his sphere because deciding the law is necessary to decide the case. If a judge pronounces upon a law without resting upon a case he steps beyond the judicial sphere and invades the legislative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding special cases, not general principles (second characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power pronounces on special cases and not upon general principles; judges decide particular points and may, by particular judgments, incidentally affect general principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgment that tends to reject all inferences from a principle can incidentally destroy that principle and still remain within ordinary limits. By contrast, a direct attack on a general principle without a particular case is beyond judicial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial passivity: inability to act except when appealed to (third characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power cannot act unless appealed to or until it has taken cognizance of an affair: the judiciary is passive by nature and must be put in motion to produce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges do not pursue crimes or investigate of their own accord; a judicial functionary who opens proceedings autonomously and usurps censorship of the laws would violate the passive nature of the authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of American judges to decide on the constitutionality of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: American judges have the recognized right to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on ordinary laws, and to refuse to apply laws they deem unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right is rooted in the American constitutional theory that the constitution is the first law and not modifiable by ordinary legislation. It gives judges immense political influence because few laws escape scrutiny; when a judge refuses to apply a law in a case that law loses part of its moral sanction and similar suits multiply until the law becomes powerless. The alternatives are that the people alter the constitution or the legislature repeals the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that laws be attacked through actual cases (procedural limitation on judicial censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to attack laws through courts of justice alone (i.e., by bringing suits) limits judicial censorship: judges contest laws only when a concrete case calling for adjudication is before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tying censorship of the laws to private interests and individual lawsuits conceals the importance of attacks from public gaze and protects legislation from wanton assailants and daily party aggressions. It focuses exposure of legislative errors on concrete, appreciable harms rather than on abstract, theoretical assaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial restraint against theoretical generalities (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge contesting laws on the ground of theoretical generalities, or opening attacks absent particular cases, would assume a political role beyond proper judicial function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If judges could attack the legislator openly and directly they might alternate between timidity and partisan boldness, attacking laws when the legislative power is weak and respecting them when it is strong; this would turn judges into political champions and menace public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of citizens to indict public functionaries before ordinary tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States all citizens have the right to indict public functionaries before ordinary tribunals; courts may judge agents of the executive when they have violated laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accessibility tends to increase respect for authorities and makes public officers more scrupulous because prosecutions are within reach of the community. Nevertheless, lawsuits are costly and difficult, so prosecutions occur only when solid grounds exist, which explains the small number of political trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction defined and the American impeachment structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Political jurisdiction is the temporary right of a political body to pronounce a legal decision. In the United States the house of representatives impeaches (arraigns) and the senate tries and awards sentence; the senate can only try persons impeached by the house, and those persons must be public functionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structure differs from European systems (e.g., house of peers or chambre des pairs) because the US senate's jurisdiction is limited to officials impeached by representatives; in Europe political bodies can try a broader class and use the penal code directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and object of American political jurisdiction: removal from office (administrative rather than penal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the primary object of political jurisdiction is to deprive a citizen of authority he has abused (removal from office), rather than to inflict penal sanctions; once removed, ordinary tribunals may then try for penalties such as imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The US senate's sentence generally terminates with removal and disqualification from office; penal consequences (liberty or life) are the province of ordinary courts and juries. The system is therefore more administrative in character than European political tribunals that may impose full penal sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction as a mild but powerful instrument of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Although American political jurisdiction is milder than European forms (it rarely imposes severe penalties), its composition and operation make it a powerful instrument in the hands of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the body that impeaches and the body that tries are composed of the same political elements and subject to the same influences, partisan impulses gain force; milder penalties increase the likelihood of conviction. The American political condemnation functions as a preventive administrative measure rather than exemplary punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: administrative prerequisites blocking prosecution of public officers (Article 75, Year VIII example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional clause requiring preliminary authorization by an administrative council (e.g., 'agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted ... by virtue of a decree of the conseil d'etat') creates a barrier to ordinary prosecutions of public officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the conseil d'etat is an administrative council dependent on the crown, victims must seek the sovereign's permission to obtain redress, enabling the sovereign to prevent punishment of his agents. This is presented as a retrogression from earlier practices where parliaments could issue warrants against public officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from broad and vague definitions of political offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Political offences described with excessive latitude (for example, Article II, Section 4: 'treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors') create risk because broad categories enable expansive use of political jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many state constitutions may be even less explicit. Broad definitions increase the latitude of political condemnation and may enable removal mechanisms to be used for partisan or preventive administrative ends rather than strictly criminal wrongdoing.
